# 
 Flink DataStream API Programming Guide
 #

In order to create your own Flink DataStream program, we encourage you to start
with anatomy of a Flink Program and gradually
add your own stream transformations. The remaining sections act as references for additional operations and advanced features.

## 
 What is a DataStream?
 #

The DataStream API gets its name from the special `DataStream` class that is
used to represent a collection of data in a Flink program. You can think of
them as immutable collections of data that can contain duplicates. This data
can either be finite or unbounded, the API that you use to work on them is the
same.

You can create an initial `DataStream` by adding a source in a Flink program.
Then you can derive new streams from this and combine them by using API methods
such as `map`, `filter`, and so on.

## 
 Anatomy of a Flink Program
 #

Flink programs look like regular programs that transform `DataStreams`. Each
program consists of the same basic parts:

- Obtain an `execution environment`,

- Load/create the initial data,

- Specify transformations on this data,

- Specify where to put the results of your computations,

- Trigger the program execution

CSV files, or using any of the other provided sources. To just read a text file
as a sequence of lines, you can use:

```

    @Override
    public Integer map(String value) {
        return Integer.parseInt(value);
    }
});

```

This will create a new DataStream by converting every String in the original
collection to an Integer.

val env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment()

val text: DataStream[String] = env.readTextFile("file:///path/to/file")

```

This will give you a DataStream on which you can then apply transformations to
create new derived DataStreams.

You apply transformations by calling methods on DataStream with a
transformation functions. For example, a map transformation looks like this:

```
val input: DataSet[String] = ...

val mapped = input.map { x => x.toInt }

```

This will create a new DataStream by converting every String in the original
collection to an Integer.

Once you have a DataStream containing your final results, you can write it to
an outside system by creating a sink. These are just some example methods for
creating a sink:

```

print()

```

Once you specified the complete program you need to trigger the program
execution by calling `execute()` on the `StreamExecutionEnvironment`.
Depending on the type of the `ExecutionEnvironment` the execution will be
triggered on your local machine or submit your program for execution on a
cluster.

The `execute()` method will wait for the job to finish and then return a
`JobExecutionResult`, this contains execution times and accumulator results.

```
final JobClient jobClient = env.executeAsync();

final JobExecutionResult jobExecutionResult = jobClient.getJobExecutionResult().get();

```

## 
 Example Program
 #

The following program is a complete, working example of streaming window word count application, that counts the
words coming from a web socket in 5 second windows. You can copy & paste the code to run it locally.

Java

public class WindowWordCount {

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();

DataStream<Tuple2<String, Integer>> dataStream = env
                .socketTextStream("localhost", 9999)
                .flatMap(new Splitter())
                .keyBy(value -> value.f0)
                .window(TumblingProcessingTimeWindows.of(Time.seconds(5)))
                .sum(1);

dataStream.print();

env.execute("Window WordCount");
    }

}

```

Scala

```

import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.scala._
import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.windowing.time.Time

object WindowWordCount {
  def main(args: Array[String]) {

val env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment
    val text = env.socketTextStream("localhost", 9999)

val counts = text.flatMap { _.toLowerCase.split("\\W+") filter { _.nonEmpty } }
      .map { (_, 1) }
      .keyBy(_._1)
      .window(TumblingProcessingTimeWindows.of(Time.seconds(5)))
      .sum(1)

counts.print()

env.execute("Window Stream WordCount")
  }
}

```

To run the example program, start the input stream with netcat first from a terminal:

```
nc -lk 9999

```

Just type some words hitting return for a new word. These will be the input to the
word count program. If you want to see counts greater than 1, type the same word again and again within
5 seconds (increase the window size from 5 seconds if you cannot type that fast ☺).

object WindowWordCount {

## 
 Data Sinks
 #

Java

Data sinks consume DataStreams and forward them to files, sockets, external systems, or print them.
Flink comes with a variety of built-in output formats that are encapsulated behind operations on the
DataStreams:

-

`writeAsText()` / `TextOutputFormat` - Writes elements line-wise as Strings. The Strings are
obtained by calling the toString() method of each element.

-

`writeAsCsv(...)` / `CsvOutputFormat` - Writes tuples as comma-separated value files. Row and field
delimiters are configurable. The value for each field comes from the toString() method of the objects.

-

-

`writeUsingOutputFormat()` / `FileOutputFormat` - Method and base class for custom file outputs. Supports
custom object-to-bytes conversion.

-

`writeToSocket` - Writes elements to a socket according to a `SerializationSchema`

-

`addSink` - Invokes a custom sink function. Flink comes bundled with connectors to other systems (such as
Apache Kafka) that are implemented as sink functions.

 Controlling Latency

Usage:

```
LocalStreamEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment();

support_records.excerpt:
Before running a streaming program in a distributed cluster, it is a good
idea to make sure that the implemented algorithm works as desired. Hence, implementing data analysis
programs is usually an incremental process of checking results, debugging, and improving.

Flink provides features to significantly ease the development process of data analysis
programs by supporting local debugging from within an IDE, injection of test data, and collection of
result data. This section give some hints how to ease the development of Flink programs.

### 
 Local Execution Environment
 #

A `LocalStreamEnvironment` starts a Flink system within the same JVM process it was created in. If you
start the LocalEnvironment from an IDE, you can set breakpoints in your code and easily debug your
program.

A LocalEnvironment is created and used as follows:

Java

```
final StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment();

DataStream<String> lines = env.addSource(/* some source */);
// build your program

env.execute();

```

Scala

```
val env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment()

val lines = env.addSource(/* some source */)
// build your program

env.execute()

```

### 
 Collection Data Sources
 #

Flink provides special data sources which are backed
by Java collections to ease testing. Once a program has been tested, the sources and sinks can be
easily replaced by sources and sinks that read from / write to external systems.

Collection data sources can be used as follows:

Java

```
final StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment();

// Create a DataStream from a list of elements
DataStream<Integer> myInts = env.fromElements(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);

// Create a DataStream from any Java collection
List<Tuple2<String, Integer>> data = ...
DataStream<Tuple2<String, Integer>> myTuples = env.fromCollection(data);

// Create a DataStream from an Iterator
Iterator<Long> longIt = ...;
DataStream<Long> myLongs = env.fromCollection(longIt, Long.class);

```

Scala

```
val env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment()

// Create a DataStream from a list of elements
val myInts = env.fromElements(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

// Create a DataStream from any Collection
val data: Seq[(String, Int)] = ...
val myTuples = env.fromCollection(data)

skill_specs.name: Checkpoint Configuration and Tuning
skill_specs.description: Configure and optimize checkpoint settings for Flink DataStream applications, including backend selection, interval tuning, and large state handling to balance fault tolerance with performance.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Set up and tune checkpointing for reliable state persistence. Select an appropriate state backend, configure checkpoint interval and timeout parameters, and apply tuning strategies for large state to achieve acceptable latency impact while maintaining fault tolerance guarantees.

## Objective

Set up and tune checkpointing for reliable state persistence
## Applicable Signals

- Initializing a new streaming job with state requirements
- Experiencing checkpoint timeouts or failures
- Optimizing recovery performance for production workloads
- Scaling state size and requiring backend optimization

## Contraindications

- Running batch-only jobs without state
- Scenarios where checkpoint overhead is not a concern or acceptable
- Applications with no fault tolerance requirements

## Intervention Moves

- Reduce checkpoint interval if recovery time is too long
- Increase checkpoint timeout if timeouts are frequent
- Switch to RocksDB backend if in-memory state exceeds available heap
- Enable incremental checkpoints for state larger than 1 GB

## Workflow Steps

- {'step': 1, 'action': 'Select state backend', 'detail': 'Choose appropriate backend (e.g., RocksDB for large state, in-memory for small state) based on state size and latency requirements'}
- {'step': 2, 'action': 'Configure checkpoint interval', 'detail': 'Set checkpoint interval to balance recovery time objective (RTO) and checkpoint overhead'}
- {'step': 3, 'action': 'Set checkpoint timeout', 'detail': 'Configure timeout threshold to prevent hanging checkpoints and trigger failure recovery'}
- {'step': 4, 'action': 'Apply large state tuning', 'detail': 'For large state, enable incremental checkpoints, tune RocksDB block cache, and configure state compaction'}
- {'step': 5, 'action': 'Validate and monitor', 'detail': 'Verify checkpoint completion rates, latency, and state size metrics; adjust parameters based on observed behavior'}

## Constraints

- Checkpoint interval must be greater than average checkpoint duration
- Timeout must be greater than checkpoint interval to allow completion
- State backend selection must match available memory and storage resources
- Large state tuning requires sufficient disk I/O capacity for incremental snapshots

## Cautions

- Aggressive checkpoint intervals may cause backpressure and reduce throughput
- Insufficient timeout values can trigger unnecessary task restarts
- RocksDB backend requires careful memory configuration to avoid out-of-memory errors
- Incremental checkpoints increase recovery complexity; validate restore procedures

## Output Contract

- Checkpoint configuration successfully applied to the DataStream job; state is persisted at configured intervals; job demonstrates acceptable latency impact and successful recovery from simulated failures

To scale a running Flink job: (1) Assess current workload and resource utilization metrics. (2) Determine target parallelism level based on demand. (3) Use savepoint to capture consistent state before scaling. (4) Adjust parallelism configuration and resubmit job from savepoint. (5) Monitor state redistribution and verify no data loss. (6) Confirm job continues processing with new resource allocation.

## Objective

Scale job resources in response to workload changes while maintaining state consistency
## Applicable Signals

- Workload increases significantly
- Workload decreases and resources are underutilized
- Resource utilization metrics indicate suboptimal allocation
- Throughput degradation detected
- Latency increases due to resource constraints

## Contraindications

- Job is in a failed or recovering state
- Scaling would violate state partitioning constraints
- No savepoint available for consistent state capture
- Job has unresolved backpressure conditions

## Constraints

## Cautions

- Ensure sufficient cluster resources are available before scaling up
- Monitor metrics during and after scaling to detect anomalies
- Verify state consistency after job restart from savepoint

## Output Contract

- Parallelism successfully adjusted
- Job continues processing with redistributed state
- No data loss confirmed
- Metrics confirm improved resource utilization or throughput aligned with scaling objective

skill_specs.name: Flink Streaming Window Word Count Setup
skill_specs.description: Initialize a Flink StreamExecutionEnvironment, ingest text from a socket source, apply flatMap tokenization, key by word, apply tumbling processing-time windows, and aggregate word counts. Use this to build basic streaming aggregation pipelines with fixed time windows.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Set up a complete Flink streaming job that reads text from a socket, tokenizes it, groups by word, applies a tumbling processing-time window, and outputs aggregated counts. Follow the pattern: create StreamExecutionEnvironment → socketTextStream → flatMap (tokenize) → keyBy (word) → window(TumblingProcessingTimeWindows) → sum(1) → print/sink → env.execute().

## Objective

Build and execute a complete streaming word-count application with windowed aggregation
## Applicable Signals

- Need to count or aggregate streaming events over fixed time intervals
- Have text or tokenizable input from a socket or file source
- Want to group results by a key field
- Require processing-time semantics (not event-time)

## Contraindications

- Require event-time semantics or watermarks
- Need session windows or sliding windows
- Input is not naturally tokenizable or keyed
- Require custom aggregation logic beyond sum

## Workflow Steps

- Create StreamExecutionEnvironment via getExecutionEnvironment()
- Attach socketTextStream source with host and port
- Apply flatMap to tokenize input (split on non-word characters, filter empty)
- Map each token to (word, 1) tuple
- Key the stream by word (f0 field)
- Apply TumblingProcessingTimeWindows with configured duration (e.g., 5 seconds)
- Aggregate using sum(1) on the count field
- Attach print() sink or custom sink
- Execute job with env.execute(jobName)

## Constraints

- Socket source must be available and listening on specified host:port
- Window duration must be positive
- Input must be line-delimited text
- Processing-time windows do not require watermarks

## Cautions

- Ensure netcat or equivalent is running on the socket before starting the job
- Window size affects latency; smaller windows produce more frequent output
- Tokenization logic (split pattern) must match input format
- Job runs indefinitely until manually stopped

## Output Contract

- Executable Flink job that prints aggregated word counts every configured window duration (e.g., 5 seconds) to stdout or sink, with format (word, count).

## Example Executions

### Example 1

- Input: Socket stream: 'hello world\nhello flink\nworld'
- Output: (hello, 1)
(world, 1)
(hello, 2)
(world, 2)
- Notes: Within a 5-second window, repeated words accumulate; new window resets counts

### Example 2

- Input: Continuous socket input over 10 seconds with window size 5s
- Output: Two separate aggregation outputs, one per window period
- Notes: Each tumbling window is independent; no overlap

skill_specs.name: Validate File Source Semantics Compatibility
skill_specs.description: Enforce exactly-once semantics awareness when using FileProcessingMode.PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY. Detect and flag the risk that full file re-processing on modification breaks exactly-once delivery guarantees. Validate configuration at setup time to prevent unintended semantics violations.
skill_specs.skill_body:
When a file-based source is configured with watchType=PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY, validate that the application's semantics requirement is compatible. If exactly-once delivery is required, warn or reject the configuration: continuous file monitoring will re-process entire file contents when modified, violating exactly-once semantics. Appending data to a file triggers full re-processing of all prior contents.

## Objective

Prevent unintended exactly-once semantics violation in continuous file monitoring
## Applicable Signals

- File-based source configured with watchType=PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY
- Application declares exactly-once delivery requirement
- File source initialization or reconfiguration event

## Contraindications

- File source is not used in the pipeline
- At-least-once or best-effort semantics is explicitly acceptable
- Files are immutable after initial write (no append or modification expected)

## Intervention Moves

- Detect watchType=PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY in file source config
- Query application semantics requirement (exactly-once vs. at-least-once vs. best-effort)
- If exactly-once required and continuous mode active: log warning and recommend mode switch or semantics relaxation
- Optionally block source initialization if conflict is unresolved

## Workflow Steps

- Inspect file source configuration for watchType setting
- Retrieve application semantics requirement declaration
- Compare watchType mode against semantics requirement
- Generate validation result with diagnostic message if conflict detected

## Constraints

- Must validate watchType setting before source activation
- Must check declared semantics guarantee against file monitoring mode
- Configuration validation must occur at setup time, not runtime

## Cautions

- Appending data to a monitored file triggers full re-processing of all prior contents
- File modifications (not just appends) trigger complete file re-read
- This constraint applies only to PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY mode; PROCESS_ONCE mode is safe for exactly-once

## Output Contract

- Configuration validated or rejected with explicit status. If conflict detected: warning logged and configuration flagged for review. If compatible: validation passes silently. Caller receives boolean pass/fail and optional diagnostic message.

## Example Executions

### Example 1

- Input: File source with watchType=PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY; application semantics=EXACTLY_ONCE
- Output: Validation fails. Warning: 'Continuous file monitoring breaks exactly-once semantics. Switch to PROCESS_ONCE or accept at-least-once delivery.'
- Notes: Conflict detected; configuration rejected or flagged for manual override.

### Example 2

- Input: File source with watchType=PROCESS_CONTINUOUSLY; application semantics=AT_LEAST_ONCE
- Output: Validation passes. No conflict.
- Notes: Semantics are compatible; continuous monitoring is safe.

### Example 3

- Input: File source with watchType=PROCESS_ONCE; application semantics=EXACTLY_ONCE
- Output: Validation passes. No conflict.
- Notes: One-time processing preserves exactly-once semantics.

- Invoke addSource(sourceFunction) for custom or external connectors

- SplittableIterator must specify the data type of returned elements
- generateSequence() produces numeric sequences only
- Custom source functions must implement the appropriate Flink source interface

- Verify connector availability before using addSource() with external systems
- Ensure type consistency across all elements in the source
- Consider parallelism and performance implications of chosen source method

skill_specs.name: Iterative Stream Loop Construction
skill_specs.description: Builds a feedback loop in a DataStream using iterate(), map/filter transformations, and closeWith() to repeatedly process elements until a termination condition is met. Enables stateful iterative computation where elements flow through a transformation body and conditionally re-enter the loop or exit to output.
skill_specs.skill_body:
1. Call iterate() on the input DataStream to create an IterativeStream.
2. Define the loop body by applying transformations (map, filter, etc.) to the IterativeStream.
3. Split the transformed stream into two parts: one to feed back via closeWith(), one to extract as final output.
4. Invoke closeWith() on the IterativeStream with the feedback branch to establish the loop.
5. Extract the output stream from the non-feedback branch.
Ensure the feedback condition eventually becomes false to prevent infinite loops.

## Objective

Construct and execute a stateful iterative computation on a DataStream
## Applicable Signals

- Input stream requires conditional re-processing
- Termination condition depends on element value or accumulated state
- Feedback loop semantics required

## Contraindications

- Single-pass transformations are sufficient
- No feedback loop or re-entry required
- Stateless map/filter operations only

## Workflow Steps

- {'step': 1, 'action': 'Create IterativeStream', 'detail': 'Call iterate() on the input DataStream to obtain an IterativeStream handle.'}
- {'step': 2, 'action': 'Define transformation body', 'detail': 'Apply map, filter, or other transformations to the IterativeStream to produce the iteration body.'}
- {'step': 3, 'action': 'Split output and feedback', 'detail': 'Use filter or other operators to partition the transformed stream into feedback (re-entry) and output (exit) branches.'}
- {'step': 4, 'action': 'Close the loop', 'detail': 'Invoke closeWith(feedbackBranch) on the IterativeStream to establish the feedback connection.'}
- {'step': 5, 'action': 'Extract final output', 'detail': 'Obtain the final DataStream from the output branch for downstream sinks or further transformations.'}

## Constraints

- Feedback branch must eventually filter out all elements to prevent infinite loops
- Output branch and feedback branch must be mutually exclusive or carefully designed to avoid data loss
- IterativeStream does not support all DataStream operations; use only map, filter, and similar transformations within the loop body

## Cautions

- Infinite loops occur if the feedback condition never becomes false; always include a termination predicate
- Performance may degrade with large iteration counts; monitor for backpressure and resource exhaustion

## Output Contract

- IterativeStream created and configured
- Loop body defined with transformations
- closeWith() invoked to route feedback
- Final output stream extracted and ready for sinks or further operations

- Output: DataStream<Long> containing only integers ≤ 0 after repeated decrement

Guides selection between -1 (maximum throughput) or small positive values (5–10 ms for low latency).
skill_specs.skill_body:
Before calling setBufferTimeout(), validate the timeout value. Reject 0 immediately. If maximizing throughput is the goal, use -1. If minimizing latency is the goal, use a small positive value such as 5 or 10 ms. Document the choice and rationale.

## Objective

prevent_performance_degradation
## Applicable Signals

- setBufferTimeout() invocation pending
- buffer timeout parameter under review
- latency or throughput optimization in progress

## Contraindications

- Not applicable when buffer timeout tuning is not required
- Do not override this rule for experimental or one-off tests without explicit risk acceptance

## Intervention Moves

- Detect timeout value = 0
- Reject or replace with safe alternative
- Log the correction and rationale
- Proceed with validated timeout value

## Workflow Steps

- Intercept setBufferTimeout() invocation with proposed timeout value
- Validate that value is not equal to 0
- If value is 0, reject and prompt for alternative
- If value is -1, accept and confirm maximum throughput mode
- If value is positive integer ≥ 5 ms, accept and confirm low-latency mode
- Log validation result and proceed with execution

## Constraints

- Buffer timeout value must be validated before execution
- Zero (0) is strictly forbidden
- Allowed values: -1 (no timeout, flush only when full) or positive integers ≥ 5 ms

## Cautions

- A buffer timeout of 0 causes severe performance degradation and should never be used
- Trade-off: -1 maximizes throughput but increases latency; small positive values (5–10 ms) minimize latency at the cost of throughput

## Output Contract

- Buffer timeout value is validated and confirmed to be either -1 or a positive integer ≥ 5 ms. Zero values are rejected or replaced. Execution proceeds with safe timeout configuration.

## Example Executions

### Example 1

- Input: setBufferTimeout(0)
- Output: Rejected; replaced with setBufferTimeout(10) for low-latency use case
- Notes: Zero timeout triggers safety rule; caller must choose throughput (-1) or latency (5–10 ms) goal

### Example 2

- Input: setBufferTimeout(-1)
- Output: Accepted; maximum throughput mode enabled
- Notes: Buffers flush only when full; suitable for batch-like or high-throughput scenarios

### Example 3

- Input: setBufferTimeout(5)
- Output: Accepted; low-latency mode enabled
- Notes: Buffers flush every 5 ms; suitable for real-time or interactive use cases

skill_specs.name: Local Streaming Program Development and Debugging
skill_specs.description: Set up and execute a Flink streaming program in a local JVM environment for incremental development, breakpoint debugging, and result validation before cluster deployment.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Create a LocalStreamEnvironment, add data sources, build your program logic, and execute locally. Use IDE breakpoints to debug algorithm behavior. Collect and inspect results before moving to cluster deployment.

## Objective

Enable local IDE-based development and debugging of Flink DataStream programs
## Applicable Signals

- Development phase initiated
- Algorithm correctness uncertain
- Incremental testing required

## Contraindications

- Running production workloads
- Testing distributed fault tolerance
- Validating cluster-specific behavior
- Processing large-scale datasets

## Workflow Steps

- {'step': 2, 'action': 'Add data source', 'detail': 'Use env.addSource() or collection-based sources (fromElements, fromCollection) to inject test data'}

- {'step': 4, 'action': 'Set breakpoints in IDE', 'detail': 'Place breakpoints in user-defined functions or operators for interactive debugging'}
- {'step': 5, 'action': 'Execute program', 'detail': 'Call env.execute() to run the program locally and trigger breakpoints'}
- {'step': 6, 'action': 'Inspect results', 'detail': 'Collect output data and validate correctness before cluster deployment'}

## Constraints

- LocalStreamEnvironment runs within a single JVM process
- Limited to local machine resources
- Not suitable for distributed state or multi-node testing

## Cautions

- LocalStreamEnvironment is not suitable for testing distributed features such as checkpointing across multiple nodes
- Memory and CPU constraints of local machine may limit testing scope
- Results from local execution may not reflect cluster-specific performance or behavior

## Output Contract

- Flink program executes locally in IDE with breakpoints active and results collected for inspection. Program completes without errors and produces expected output artifacts.

- Notes: Basic setup for local testing with collection-based data source

- Output: Program pauses at breakpoint in IDE, allowing inspection of intermediate values
- Notes: Interactive debugging workflow for algorithm validation

skill_specs.name: Collection-Based Test Data Injection
skill_specs.description: Create DataStream instances from Java collections, lists, or iterators for unit testing and validation without external data sources. Enables isolated testing of transformation logic with known inputs by injecting test data directly into the streaming pipeline.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Use this skill to populate a Flink DataStream with test elements from Java collections. Call the appropriate method based on your test data structure: fromElements() for inline element lists, fromCollection() for Java collections, or fromCollection(iterator, class) for iterators. The resulting DataStream is ready for downstream operators and assertions.

## Objective

Inject test data into a Flink DataStream for isolated testing
## Applicable Signals

- Test phase initiated
- Need for deterministic input data
- Local or IDE-based debugging session
- Incremental algorithm validation

## Contraindications

- Testing with large datasets that exceed memory
- Simulating real-time data arrival patterns or timing behavior
- Validating backpressure and windowing behavior under load
- Production data pipeline execution

## Workflow Steps

- {'step': 1, 'action': 'Create a LocalStreamEnvironment', 'detail': 'Call StreamExecutionEnvironment.createLocalEnvironment() to set up the local execution context'}
- {'step': 2, 'action': 'Choose data source method based on input type', 'detail': 'Select fromElements() for inline values, fromCollection() for Java collections, or fromCollection(iterator, class) for iterators'}
- {'step': 3, 'action': 'Invoke the selected method on the environment', 'detail': 'Pass test data or collection reference to create the DataStream'}
- {'step': 4, 'action': 'Chain downstream operators', 'detail': 'Apply transformations, filters, or other operators to the returned DataStream'}
- {'step': 5, 'action': 'Execute and validate', 'detail': 'Call env.execute() and assert results match expected output'}

## Constraints

- Data must fit in memory as a Java collection or iterator
- LocalStreamEnvironment must be created first
- Test data must be serializable by Flink's type system

## Cautions

- Collection-based sources are not suitable for performance or scale testing
- Watermark and event-time semantics may not be accurately simulated with static collections
- Use only in development and testing environments

## Output Contract

- Returns a DataStream<T> object populated with test elements, ready for downstream operators and test assertions. The DataStream is fully typed and compatible with all standard Flink transformations.

## Example Executions

### Example 1

- Input: Inline integer elements: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
- Output: DataStream<Integer> myInts = env.fromElements(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
- Notes: Simplest form for small, homogeneous test datasets

### Example 2

- Input: Java List of tuples: List<Tuple2<String, Integer>> data
- Output: DataStream<Tuple2<String, Integer>> myTuples = env.fromCollection(data)
- Notes: Suitable for structured test records with multiple fields

### Example 3

- Input: Iterator<Long> longIt with Long.class type hint
- Output: DataStream<Long> myLongs = env.fromCollection(longIt, Long.class)
- Notes: Allows lazy evaluation and type specification for generic iterators

skill_specs.description: Asynchronously collect DataStream output into an Iterator for testing and debugging. Provides a non-blocking handoff of streaming results to client code for inspection and validation.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Call collectAsync() on a DataStream to retrieve results as an Iterator. Use this micro-skill when you need to inspect or validate streaming output in a test or debug context. The Iterator allows you to iterate over collected tuples or records without blocking the stream.

## Objective

retrieve streaming results for inspection and validation
## Applicable Signals

- need to inspect or validate DataStream output
- test or debug context active
- results are small enough to fit in memory
- non-blocking collection required

## Contraindications

- production high-throughput pipelines
- large result sets that exceed available memory
- real-time sinks required for external systems
- parallel execution needed

## Workflow Steps

- {'step': 4, 'action': 'Iterate over results', 'detail': 'Use standard Iterator methods (hasNext(), next()) to inspect collected output.'}

- collectAsync() returns an Iterator; caller must iterate to consume results
- collection is asynchronous; caller should handle timing appropriately
- suitable only for small result sets due to in-memory collection
- not intended for persistent or external data sinks

## Cautions

- Do not use in production pipelines with high throughput or large volumes.
- Ensure result set fits in available memory before calling collectAsync().

- Caller can iterate over results to inspect or validate output

- Output: Iterator<Tuple2<String, Integer>> myOutput = myResult.collectAsync();
- Notes: Java example with generic type parameters.

skill_specs.name: Create DataStream from Collection with Serialization Constraint
skill_specs.description: Initialize a DataStream from an Iterator or collection source, respecting serialization requirements and single-parallelism execution model. Used for bootstrapping streaming jobs from test data or small reference datasets.
skill_specs.skill_body:
Call env.fromCollection(iterator) to create a DataStream from an in-memory collection. Ensure all data types and iterators implement Serializable. Note that collection data sources execute with parallelism = 1 and cannot be parallelized.

## Objective

instantiate DataStream from in-memory collection
## Applicable Signals

- development or testing phase
- data available in memory as Iterator or collection
- all elements are Serializable

## Contraindications

- large datasets
- parallel execution required
- non-serializable objects in collection
- production data ingestion from external sources

## Workflow Steps

- Verify all data types and iterators in the collection implement Serializable
- Call env.fromCollection(iterator) or env.fromCollection(collection)
- Receive DataStream object
- Proceed to transformation or sink operations

## Constraints

- All data types must implement Serializable
- All iterators must implement Serializable
- Execution parallelism is fixed at 1; cannot be increased

## Cautions

- Collection data sources cannot be executed in parallel
- Serialization failures will occur at runtime if objects are not Serializable

## Output Contract

- DataStream object ready for downstream transformation or sink operations; parallelism is 1

## Example Executions

### Example 1

- Input: Iterator[Long] containing numeric values
- Output: DataStream[Long] with parallelism = 1
- Notes: val longIt: Iterator[Long] = ...; val myLongs = env.fromCollection(longIt)
